idiom_name: hand-written enrich step: key extraction + SQLite/hash lookup + struct field merge
implementation_notes: C has no messaging or resource framework, so the enricher is a function: read the lookup key out of the parsed message, resolve the missing fields from a resource - a prepared SQLite statement, an in-memory hash table or a file - and write them into the message struct before it is handed to the next stage. Put the resource behind a small accessor (function pointers or an opaque handle) so the enrichment logic can be tested with a stub; ownership of merged strings and error handling stay explicit because nothing in the language does either for you. The full 'component' shape (an enricher object holding a datasource handle) only pays off when several enrichment steps share one connection or cache.
pitfalls: Every merged string needs a defined owner: fields filled with strdup() leak when the message is released with free(msg) alone - pair each message with an explicit release function.
A failed lookup must be distinguishable from an empty value: return a status enum, never a zeroed struct, or consumers cannot tell 'unknown' from 'empty'.

SQLite's threading mode decides whether a connection may be shared: in multi-thread mode a single connection must not be used by two threads at once - keep one connection per thread or serialize access, and finalize every prepared statement on all paths.
